newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Gold-Low prices, high cost threaten.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Gold-Low prices, high cost threaten.

text.p: A sustained low period for gold prices together with increasing mine operating costs could put a ceiling on growth in Australian gold production by the end of the decade, research by Australia's chief government forecasting agency shows.
Internationaly, gold continues to languish at or near three year lows of around US$342 an ounce, down from US$417 about a year ago.
In Australian dollar terms, the Australian Bureau of Agricutural and Resource Economics (ABARE) expects the gold to fall to an average A$472 an ounce by 2001/02 from A$478 in 1996/97.
The Perth Mint on Friday quoted spot gold at A$448.53 an ounce.

The fall in the Australian dollar price of gold is likely to reflect a period of decline in the real U.S. dollar gold price, tempered somewhat by more favourable currency exchange rates for the Australian sector.

Expectations of growth in Australian gold production, which should lift output to about 336 tonnes by 1999/2000 from a projected 303 tonnes in 1996/97, reflects the exploitation of existing gold mine projects and the number of committed new projects, Simon Middleton, ABARE gold analyst told an industry conference this week.
The increase has been helped by exploration spending which aided in establishing many of the large scale finds in Western Australia.

These include the Super Pit, 50-50 owned by Gold Mines of Kalgoorlie Ltd and Homestake Mining Co, which is expected to ramp up production to nearly 600,000 ounces and the Bronzewing mine, owned by Great Central Mines NL and Plutonic Resources Ltd's Plutonic deposit, both of which by 2000 are forecast to be producing some 400,000 ounces annually.

But by the end of the decade, higher Australian mining costs, estimated to average around A$380 an ounce would become a reality for miners as maturing deposits force them to dig deeper open cut mines and initiate more underground operations.
"Expanding costs and easing real gold prices are expected to influence the capacity of higher cost operations to maintain current production," Middleton said.
Currently, nine percent of Australian gold was produced at costs above the 1996 average Australian gold price of A$498 an ounce.
"At A$460 an ounce, 17 percent, or almost 50 tonnes of present production, has cash costs greater than this price," he said.

The increase in exploration was linked to a rapid increase total real gross industry margins to A$1.01 billion in 1994 from A$$480 million in the early 1990s, driven by the rise in real cash margins to A$201 an ounce from A$193 over the same period, ABARE figures show.

"The high levels of exploration expenditure resulted in Australia's economically demonstrated reserves of gold expanding to 4,263 tonnes in 1995 from 2,129 tonnes in 1991, reserves on which production growth in the next three years will be principaly based," Middleton said.
But the real cash margins of the Australian industry are now projected to fall to A$91 an ounce from A$131 in calendar 1996, which threatens to cause exploration spending to decline.

"The expected fall in exploration expenditure is projected to result in a decline in the growth of Australian production due to a slowdown in the rate of new discovery of new deposits," Middleton said.
About 44 percent of currently operating gold projects are expected to exhaust current resrve bases by 2000 unless additional reserves are discovered, he said.
However, the Australian gold mining sector has the capacity to absorb potential cost increases by applying new technologies, Middleton added.
"About 27 percent of the projected producion level in 2001/02 is expected to come from as yet unannounced sources," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
